To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the decoupling of dark matter from standard model particles occurs at a temperature of about 1.2 MeV, that the corresponding decoupling time is about 2.4 × 10−4 s, that dark matter decouples at an average velocity of about 0.5 × 10^5 cm/s, and that the decoupled dark matter particles have an average velocity of 0.2 × 10^-3 cm/s.

(i) the decoupling temperature is always smaller than the WIMP mass, (ii) the decoupled WIMPs are colder than the standard thermal relic density would suggest, and (iii) the decouplings of the lightest Kaluz–Klein and supersymmetric particle occur at temperatures that are very different from each other.

(1) the decoupling temperature is a function of the scattering amplitude only, and not of the WIMP mass, (2) the decoupled WIMP number density is a function of its mass only, and not the scattering amplitude, and (3) the decouplings are not instantaneous but occur on a timescale that is determined by the scattering amplitude.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question how the thermal decoupling of the dark matter from the standard model radiation affects the formation of the smallest dark matter structures.
the question how dark matter decoupled from the thermal plasma in the early universe.
the evolution of the dark matter distribution function in the early universe.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the decoupling process is not as important as it is often believed.
, for a large class of dark matter candidates, the smallest gravitationically bound objects are still much too small to be detected by current or planned facilities.
the thermal decoupling of dark matter is a very complex process that can only be understood in full detail from first principles.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the thermal decoupling of the WIMPs is not just a simple cut-off, but it is rather a process which is determined by the underlying particle physics model.
the decoupling temperature is a very important cosmological scale and that its determination is a necessary prerequisite for any cosmological application of WIMP models.

the thermal decoupling of the dark matter from the standard model is a very subtle and important process that can have a strong impact for the smallest dark matter structures as well as for the indirect detection prospects.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the decoupling of dark matter from the thermal bath can be determined with high precision and without relying on approximations.

, for a large range of parameters, the thermal decoupling scale is much smaller than the temperature of big bang nucleosynthesis and that the corresponding small scale cut-off is therefore well below the scale of the smallest galaxies that are observed today.
the thermal decoupling scale can be as high as ~10 MeV in the case of a lightest supersymmetric neutralino, and as low as ~1 MeV for the lightest Kalua–Klein particle.
